opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think about it a lot, because the bottleneck is shifting. For most of history, producing information was expensive: writing the report, doing the analysis, drafting the code. Now the cost of generating information is collapsing toward zero, so the scarce resource becomes attention and judgment. The skills that matter are the ones that help you decide what deserves your attention and what to do with it.

The first one I'd point to is **discernment**, or taste. When you can get ten drafts or ten analyses in a minute, the hard part isn't producing the answer, it's recognizing which one is actually good, and why. That means you still need real domain knowledge. There's a temptation to think "the AI knows things, so I don't have to," but it's the opposite. You need enough depth to catch when something is subtly wrong, because these systems are very good at being confidently plausible.

The second is **knowing what you actually want**. A lot of people underestimate how hard it is to articulate a goal clearly. With AI, specification becomes the work. If you can describe precisely what outcome you're after, what the constraints are, and what "done" looks like, you get enormous leverage. If you can't, you get a lot of fast, polished output pointed in the wrong direction. So clear thinking and clear writing are becoming more valuable, not less.

Third, and this one is more personal, is **emotional regulation and managing your own attention**. More throughput means more inputs, more notifications, more options, more things you *could* be doing. If you don't have a stable relationship with your own mind, it's really easy to get overwhelmed or to spend your day reacting. Being able to notice when you're anxious or scattered, stay grounded, and choose deliberately what to focus on is going to be a huge differentiator. I'd honestly put things like meditation or any practice that builds self-awareness in the same category as technical skills now.

Fourth is **verification and epistemic hygiene**: a habit of asking "how do I know this is true?" Checking sources, running the code, looking at the actual data. As the volume of generated content grows, the people who maintain good epistemic habits will be the ones others trust.

And finally, I'd say **adaptability**: being willing to keep rebuilding your workflows. The tools change every few months. The people who thrive aren't necessarily the ones who master one tool, they're the ones who stay curious and keep experimenting, and who don't tie their identity too tightly to a particular way of working.

If I had to compress all of that, it's this: the machines are getting very good at generating, so humans need to get very good at *choosing*: what to ask for, what to trust, what to pay attention to, and what actually matters to them.

r001.rationale: The response recommends discernment, self-awareness, verification, and adaptability, but does not connect these skills to generalizing across domains.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim that the AI era is the best time in human history to be a generalist.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the bottleneck moves. For most of history, the scarce thing was getting information. Now the scarce thing is deciding what to do with it. And I think that shifts what matters toward a few things.

The first one is judgment, and specifically the ability to evaluate an answer you didn't produce yourself. If a model hands you a summary, a piece of code, a market analysis, you need enough grounding in the domain to know whether it smells right. That's a different skill than generating it. It's closer to being an editor than a writer, or a reviewer than a researcher. And I don't think you can skip the part where you learned the fundamentals, because that's where the taste comes from. People who never struggled through the underlying work don't have the error-detection reflex.

The second thing is asking good questions. When throughput is cheap, the quality of your output is mostly determined by the quality of your prompt, in the broadest sense. What problem are you actually solving? What constraints matter? What would a wrong answer look like? Most people are surprisingly bad at articulating what they want, and that used to be hidden because the slow part was execution. Now it's exposed.

Third, I'd say synthesis across domains. The models are very good at going deep in a lane you point them at. The thing humans still do well is notice that a problem in one field rhymes with something in another, and bring those together. That takes breadth and curiosity more than specialization.

And then maybe the underrated one is attention management. If information throughput goes up ten or a hundred times, the person who can decide what not to look at wins. The skill isn't consuming more. It's being deliberate about what gets your focus and being comfortable letting the rest go.

So I'd summarize it as: get good enough at something to have real taste, learn to frame problems precisely, read widely, and guard your attention. None of that is new advice, honestly. It's just that the penalty for not doing it got a lot steeper.

r001.rationale: The response recommends synthesis across domains, breadth, and curiosity, but does not clearly describe metacognitive skills as enabling that generalization.

r002.rationale: It recommends breadth and cross-domain synthesis, but never claims this is the best time in human history to be a generalist.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most valuable skills is going to be asking good questions. As AI makes it easier to get information and produce work, the bottleneck shifts toward deciding what’s worth understanding and what’s worth doing.

That also makes judgment more important. Can you look at an answer and identify the assumptions behind it? Can you tell what evidence would actually change your mind? You need enough depth in a subject to recognize when something sounds convincing but doesn’t hold up.

And then there’s managing your attention. Increasing information throughput doesn’t automatically increase understanding. You still need time to sit with an idea, connect it to what you already know, and decide whether it matters. I’d practice using AI to explore different perspectives, while also making yourself articulate your own view. That process of forming a view, testing it, and updating it is a skill that remains valuable even as the tools get much better.

r001.rationale: The response recommends judgment and reflecting on assumptions and evidence, but does not connect these metacognitive skills to generalizing across domains.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim that the AI era is the best time in human history to be a generalist.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most valuable skills is learning how to learn—and, specifically, how to recognize when your understanding of something needs to change. If AI dramatically increases the amount of information available to us, the bottleneck becomes our ability to make sense of it: to ask good questions, evaluate the answers, and connect them to what we already know.

That makes critical thinking really important. Can you distinguish a convincing explanation from a well-supported one? Can you identify the assumptions behind an answer? And can you sit with uncertainty long enough to investigate, rather than immediately accepting whatever sounds plausible?

I’d also emphasize attention and judgment. More information doesn’t automatically produce better decisions. You need some sense of what you’re trying to accomplish and which information actually matters. Being able to step back, decide what’s worth focusing on, and then use AI to explore it seems much more valuable than trying to keep up with everything.

r001.rationale: The response recommends learning how to learn and monitoring when understanding needs to change, but does not clearly connect those skills to generalizing across domains.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim that the AI era is the best time in human history to be a generalist.
